Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis. It is one of the most common and economically significant diseases of apple trees worldwide, affecting leaves, fruit, and occasionally young shoots.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety or scab-like lesions on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Infected leaves may turn yellow and drop prematurely
Dark, scabby, corky lesions on fruit surfaces
Fruit may be deformed or cracked in severe infections
Young shoot infections cause rough, scabby bark
prevention: Plant resistant apple varieties when possible
Prune trees to improve air circulation and reduce humidity
Rake and remove fallen leaves promptly to reduce fungal spore sources
Apply protective fungicides before and during wet periods in spring
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of trees
Apple___Apple_scab.management: Confirm diagnosis with a local agricultural extension officer or plant pathologist. Management typically involves a combination of cultural practices (sanitation, pruning) and fungicide applications timed to match the infection risk periods.

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot of apple is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It affects leaves, fruit, and bark, and can be a serious problem in orchards with poor sanitation or stressed trees.
symptoms: Circular leaf spots with purple or reddish margins and tan or brown centers (frog-eye appearance)
Fruit rot starting as small purple or reddish spots that enlarge to black, mummified fruit
Cankers on branches showing dead, sunken bark
prevention: Remove and destroy mummified fruit and dead wood
Prune out infected branches during dry weather
Maintain tree vigor through proper fertilization and watering
Apply fungicides during the growing season
Avoid wounding tree bark
Apple___Black_rot.management: Contact a local agricultural expert for confirmation and advice on registered fungicide schedules. Cultural practices such as sanitation and removal of infected material are essential.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is caused by the fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. It requires two host plants: apple (or crabapple) and eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) or other junipers.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surfaces in spring and early summer
Spots may have red or orange margins
Tube-like structures (aecia) develop on the undersides of leaves
Infected fruit shows similar orange spots and may drop early
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Remove nearby juniper or red cedar trees if practical
Apply protective fungicides in spring when conditions favor spore release
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.management: This disease requires management on both host plants. Fungicide applications on apple are timed to the period when juniper galls are releasing spores. Consult a local horticultural expert.

Apple___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy apple plant based on the model's training data. Healthy apple leaves are typically dark green, smooth, and free from spots, lesions, or discoloration.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
Leaf color, shape, and texture appear within normal range for this crop
prevention: Continue regular monitoring of your plants
Maintain appropriate watering, fertilization, and pruning practices
Scout regularly for early signs of pests or disease
Apple___healthy.management: Continue good orchard hygiene practices. Monitor regularly and consult a local agricultural expert if any changes in plant appearance are observed.

Blueberry___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy blueberry plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
Leaf appears within normal range for blueberry
prevention: Maintain appropriate soil pH (4.5–5.5 for blueberries)
Ensure good drainage and adequate moisture
Monitor for pests and diseases regularly
Blueberry___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring and good cultural practices. Consult a local expert if symptoms appear.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew of cherry is caused by Podosphaera clandestina. It is one of the most widespread cherry diseases, favored by warm, dry weather with high humidity.
symptoms: White to gray powdery fungal growth on young leaves and shoots
Infected leaves may curl, pucker, or become distorted
Severe infections can cause early leaf drop
Young fruit may become infected, developing a russeted appearance
prevention: Plant in well-ventilated locations with good air circulation
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes lush, susceptible growth
Prune trees to improve airflow
Apply fungicides preventively during periods of rapid growth in spring
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.management: Consult a local agricultural authority for registered fungicide recommendations. Sulfur-based products and other fungicides are commonly used.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy cherry plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Monitor regularly for early signs of disease or pest activity
Maintain good orchard hygiene and balanced nutrition
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local expert if symptoms appear.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot of corn is caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis. It is a significant fungal disease in many maize-growing regions, particularly where conservation tillage practices leave crop residues on the soil surface.
symptoms: Rectangular, tan to gray lesions that run parallel to leaf veins
Lesions are typically narrow (2–4 mm) and elongated
Lesions may coalesce to blight entire leaves in severe cases
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids
Rotate crops — avoid continuous corn on the same land
Reduce crop residue on the soil surface through tillage where appropriate
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.management: Consult a local agronomist for hybrid selection and fungicide recommendations. Foliar fungicide applications may be economical in high-risk fields.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust of corn is caused by Puccinia sorghi. It is a widespread disease found wherever corn is grown.
symptoms: Small, round to elongated, cinnamon-brown to brick-red pustules scattered over leaf surfaces
Pustules are found on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
As pustules mature they may turn dark brown to black
Heavy infections cause general yellowing and early senescence of leaves
prevention: Plant rust-resistant hybrids — this is the most effective approach
Early planting can allow the crop to mature before peak rust pressure in some regions
Monitor fields regularly to detect early infection
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.management: Consult a local agronomist to determine whether fungicide applications are economically justified based on hybrid susceptibility, growth stage, and local disease pressure.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight (NLB) of corn is caused by Exserohilum turcicum. It is an important foliar disease that can cause significant yield losses in susceptible hybrids.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped lesions, typically 2.5–15 cm in length
Lesions are initially grayish-green, becoming tan to light brown at maturity
In humid conditions, dark gray-green sporulation may appear within lesions
Severe infections can blight entire leaves
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids
Rotate crops to reduce inoculum buildup in corn residue
Tillage to bury crop residue can reduce disease carryover
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.management: Consult a local agronomist for hybrid selection guidance. Fungicide applications may be warranted in susceptible hybrids at or near tasseling when disease pressure is high.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy corn plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Maintain appropriate plant population, fertilization, and irrigation
Scout regularly and rotate crops to manage disease risk
Corn_(maize)___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local agronomist if symptoms appear.

Grape___Black_rot.description: Grape black rot is caused by Guignardia bidwellii. It is one of the most destructive diseases of grapes in humid regions, capable of destroying entire crops if not managed.
symptoms: Reddish-brown circular spots on leaves, with tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) visible within spots
Infected berries shrivel and turn into hard, black, mummified fruit that remain attached to the cluster
Young shoot and tendril infections show dark, elongated lesions
prevention: Remove and destroy mummified fruit and infected canes during pruning
Prune to improve air circulation within the canopy
Apply protective fungicides beginning at bud break through fruit set
Avoid overhead irrigation
Grape___Black_rot.management: Black rot requires a comprehensive fungicide spray program beginning early in the season. Consult your local agricultural extension service for a recommended spray schedule.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca (Black Measles) is a complex wood disease of grapevines caused by a consortium of fungal pathogens including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Fomitiporia mediterranea. It is a chronic, progressive disease with no cure.
symptoms: Tiger-striping pattern on leaves: interveinal chlorosis progressing to necrosis
Leaf margins may dry and die (marginal leaf scorch)
Berries develop small dark spots and may shrivel
Sudden collapse of the whole vine can occur (apoplexy)
prevention: Use certified disease-free planting material
Prune during dry weather and protect pruning wounds with wound sealants
Avoid large pruning wounds — use double-pruning techniques
Remove and destroy severely infected vines
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).management: There is no effective cure for Esca once a vine is infected. Management focuses on slowing disease spread. Consult a local viticulture expert for guidance.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Grape leaf blight caused by Isariopsis clavispora produces dark spots on leaves and is mainly found in warm, humid viticultural regions.
symptoms: Dark brown to black irregular spots on leaves
Spots may coalesce causing large areas of necrosis
Infected leaves may drop prematurely
prevention: Improve air circulation through canopy management and pruning
Avoid overhead irrigation
Remove infected fallen leaves
Apply fungicides where disease pressure is consistently high
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.management: Consult a local viticulture expert for diagnosis confirmation and management recommendations appropriate to your region.

Grape___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy grapevine based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Maintain appropriate canopy management and pruning
Monitor regularly for early disease and pest signs
Use certified disease-free planting material
Grape___healthy.management: Continue good vineyard hygiene and regular monitoring. Consult a local viticulture expert if symptoms appear.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB), also known as citrus greening, is caused by the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. It is transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid insect and is considered the most devastating citrus disease worldwide. There is currently no cure.
symptoms: Asymmetric yellowing (blotchy mottle) of leaves — unlike the uniform yellowing of nutrient deficiencies
Small, lopsided, misshapen fruit with bitter taste
Fruit may remain green at the end opposite the stem
Twig dieback and overall decline of the tree
prevention: Strictly control the Asian citrus psyllid vector through monitoring and management
Use certified disease-free nursery stock
Immediately remove and destroy infected trees to prevent spread
Report suspected cases to your local plant health authority — HLB is a notifiable disease in many countries
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).management: There is no cure for HLB. Contact your local agricultural or plant health authority immediately if HLB is suspected. It is a notifiable disease requiring mandatory reporting and quarantine measures in many regions.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of peach is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It affects leaves, fruit, and shoots and is common in humid peach-growing regions.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that become angular, dark brown to purple-brown lesions
Infected leaf tissue may fall out leaving shot-hole appearance
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely
Fruit shows small, water-soaked lesions that become dark and sunken
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation
Apply copper-based bactericides preventively starting at bud swell
Prune infected shoots during dry weather
Peach___Bacterial_spot.management: Consult a local agricultural expert for confirmation and spray program recommendations. Copper sprays are commonly used. Integrated management combining cultural practices and appropriately timed sprays is recommended.

Peach___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy peach plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Monitor regularly for signs of bacterial spot, brown rot, and peach leaf curl
Maintain good tree nutrition and drainage
Peach___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local expert if symptoms appear.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of pepper is caused by Xanthomonas euvesicatoria and related species. It is a common and damaging disease in warm, humid pepper-producing regions.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked circular to irregular spots on leaves that turn brown and may have yellow halos
Severe infections cause extensive leaf yellowing and defoliation
Fruit shows raised, scabby, brown lesions that reduce marketability
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed or seed treated with hot water
Plant resistant varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation
Rotate crops — avoid planting pepper in fields with recent bacterial spot history
Apply copper-based bactericides preventively
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.management: Consult a local agricultural expert for a recommended spray program. Copper resistance in Xanthomonas populations is increasing — your local extension service can advise on the most effective current management options.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy bell pepper plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Monitor regularly for early signs of bacterial spot and virus diseases
Maintain good drainage and air circulation
Pepper,_bell___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local expert if symptoms appear.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Potato early blight is primarily caused by Alternaria solani. It is a widespread fungal disease that typically affects older, lower leaves first, especially under conditions of stress or poor nutrition.
symptoms: Dark brown to black circular spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older leaves
Surrounding tissue may turn yellow
Lesions typically appear first on older, lower leaves
Severe infection can cause premature defoliation
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes
Maintain adequate plant nutrition — nitrogen deficiency increases susceptibility
Rotate crops and avoid continuous potato production on the same land
Improve air circulation; avoid dense planting
Apply protective fungicides during periods of high risk
Potato___Early_blight.management: Consult a local agricultural expert to confirm diagnosis and recommend appropriate fungicide options. Cultural practices including crop rotation and proper fertilization are important components of management.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Potato late blight is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans. It is historically one of the most devastating plant diseases (responsible for the Irish Potato Famine) and can destroy an entire crop rapidly under favorable conditions.
symptoms: Dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves that expand rapidly
White, downy fungal growth visible on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Brown, firm, rotting lesions on tubers
Entire plants may collapse and die rapidly in cool, wet weather
prevention: Plant certified, disease-free seed potatoes
Plant resistant or tolerant varieties
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the soil level
Apply protective fungicides preventively during cool, wet periods
Monitor fields closely and destroy infected plants promptly
Potato___Late_blight.management: Late blight can spread extremely rapidly. Contact a local agricultural expert or agricultural authority promptly if late blight is suspected. This disease may require mandatory reporting in some regions.

Potato___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy potato plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes
Monitor regularly for early and late blight
Rotate crops and maintain proper nutrition
Potato___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local expert if symptoms appear.

Raspberry___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy raspberry plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Monitor regularly for gray mold, cane diseases, and virus symptoms
Prune out old canes after fruiting to improve air circulation
Raspberry___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local expert if symptoms appear.

Soybean___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy soybean plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Rotate crops and use certified seed
Monitor for sudden death syndrome, soybean cyst nematode, and frogeye leaf spot
Soybean___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local agronomist if symptoms appear.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew of squash and cucurbits is caused by Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum. It is one of the most common diseases of cucurbits worldwide.
symptoms: White to gray powdery fungal growth on leaf surfaces (typically upper surface first)
Affected leaves may turn yellow, brown, and dry out
In severe cases, the entire leaf surface may be covered with white powder
Stems and petioles may also be infected
prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available
Maintain good spacing to improve air circulation
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
Apply fungicides preventively if disease pressure is historically high
Squash___Powdery_mildew.management: Consult a local agricultural expert for appropriate fungicide recommendations. Sulfur-based and biological fungicides are commonly used.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Strawberry leaf scorch is caused by Diplocarpon earliana. It is a common fungal disease that can be severe in wet, humid seasons.
symptoms: Numerous small, irregular, dark purple spots on leaf surfaces
Spots may coalesce giving leaves a scorched or burned appearance
Affected leaves may dry out and die
Severe infections weaken plants and reduce fruit yield
prevention: Plant in well-drained locations with good air circulation
Use certified disease-free planting material
Remove and destroy old plant debris after harvest
Apply fungicides during wet periods if disease pressure is high
Avoid overhead irrigation where possible
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.management: Consult a local agricultural expert for fungicide recommendations. Cultural practices including proper site selection, plant spacing, and debris removal are important management components.

Strawberry___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy strawberry plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Use certified disease-free planting stock
Monitor regularly for leaf diseases and gray mold
Maintain good air circulation and drainage
Strawberry___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local expert if symptoms appear.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of tomato is caused by Xanthomonas species. It affects leaves, stems, and fruit and is common in warm, humid tomato-growing regions.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that become dark brown or black with yellow halos
Spots may have a greasy appearance initially
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and drop
Fruit develops small, raised, scabby, brown spots reducing marketability
prevention: Use certified disease-free or treated seed
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation
Plant resistant varieties where available
Rotate tomatoes out of fields with disease history
Apply copper-based bactericides preventively in humid conditions
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.management: Consult a local agricultural expert for confirmation and spray program recommendations. Copper resistance is a growing concern; your local extension service can advise on current best management options.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Tomato early blight is primarily caused by Alternaria solani. It is a common fungal disease that first affects older, lower leaves and can cause significant defoliation.
symptoms: Dark brown, circular lesions with concentric rings (target-board appearance) on older leaves
Yellow halo may surround the lesion
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, starting from the bottom of the plant
Stem lesions (collar rot) may occur near the soil line in young plants
prevention: Rotate crops — avoid planting tomatoes in the same location year after year
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
Water at the base of plants; avoid wetting foliage
Stake plants to improve air circulation
Apply protective fungicides during periods of high disease risk
Tomato___Early_blight.management: Consult a local agricultural expert for fungicide recommendations. Maintaining plant health through adequate fertilization and watering reduces susceptibility to early blight.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Tomato late blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans, the same pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine. It can devastate tomato crops rapidly in cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Large, irregular, dark green to brown water-soaked lesions on leaves
White, moldy growth visible on underside of leaves in humid conditions
Brown, firm lesions on stems
Fruit develops greasy-looking, dark brown lesions and rots rapidly
prevention: Plant certified disease-free transplants
Use resistant tomato varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly — do not compost them
Apply protective fungicides before disease onset in high-risk weather
Tomato___Late_blight.management: Late blight spreads extremely rapidly. Contact a local agricultural expert immediately if suspected. Remove and destroy (do not compost) infected plants.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold is caused by Passalora fulva. It primarily affects tomatoes grown in greenhouses or tunnels where humidity is high.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Corresponding olive-green to grayish-brown, velvety fungal growth on the lower leaf surface
Infected leaves may curl upward and eventually dry out
prevention: Improve greenhouse ventilation to reduce humidity
Avoid overhead watering
Space plants adequately for air circulation
Use resistant tomato varieties where available
Remove infected leaves promptly
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.management: Consult a local agricultural expert or protected cropping specialist for fungicide and management recommendations appropriate to your growing environment.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot of tomato is caused by Septoria lycopersici. It is one of the most common tomato diseases and progresses from the bottom of the plant upward.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots with dark brown borders and lighter tan or gray centers
Tiny dark dots (pycnidia) visible within the center of lesions
Spots first appear on older, lower leaves
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop, progressively working up the plant
prevention: Rotate tomatoes with non-solanaceous crops (at least 2–3 years)
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after the growing season
Avoid wetting foliage — use drip irrigation or water at the base
Stake or cage plants to improve air circulation
Apply protective fungicides when conditions are humid
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.management: Consult a local agricultural expert for fungicide recommendations. Maintaining plant health and minimizing leaf wetness are key management components.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae) is an arachnid pest that can cause severe damage to tomatoes and many other crops, particularly in hot, dry conditions.
symptoms: Tiny yellow or white stippling (speckled) spots on leaf surfaces caused by mite feeding
Leaves may turn bronze, yellow, or brown and eventually drop
Fine webbing visible on leaves and between stems in heavy infestations
Small moving dots (mites) visible on leaf undersides with magnification
prevention: Monitor for spider mites regularly, especially on the undersides of leaves
Maintain adequate plant moisture — drought stress increases mite susceptibility
Encourage natural predators (predatory mites, ladybirds)
Avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes lush growth attractive to mites
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.management: This is a pest management issue, not a fungal disease. Consult a local agricultural expert for mite management options appropriate to your crop and region. Options may include biological control (predatory mites), horticultural oils, or appropriate miticides.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot of tomato is caused by Corynespora cassiicola. It is found in tropical and subtropical regions and has become increasingly common in some temperate regions.
symptoms: Circular to irregular brown lesions with concentric rings giving a target-like appearance
Lesions may have yellow halos and affect all above-ground plant parts
Dark brown spots on fruit
Severe infections can cause significant defoliation
prevention: Rotate crops and remove infected crop debris
Improve air circulation through staking and pruning
Avoid overhead irrigation
Apply preventive fungicides during high-risk periods
Tomato___Target_Spot.management: Consult a local agricultural expert for fungicide recommendations and to confirm the diagnosis, as target spot can resemble other tomato leaf diseases.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a begomovirus transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. It is one of the most damaging tomato viruses worldwide, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of leaves (leaves curl upward from the margins)
Leaf yellowing (chlorosis), particularly at leaf margins and interveinal areas
Stunted plant growth
Severe flower drop and drastic reduction in fruit set
Infected plants have a characteristic bushy, stunted appearance
prevention: Use TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato varieties — this is the most effective approach
Control the whitefly vector rigorously using yellow sticky traps, reflective mulches, and appropriate insecticides
Use insect-proof screens in nurseries
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.management: There is no cure for TYLCV in infected plants. Management focuses on preventing infection through vector control and resistant varieties. Consult a local agricultural expert for integrated pest management recommendations for whitefly control.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is a mechanically transmitted tobamovirus. It is highly contagious and spreads through contact with contaminated tools, hands, and plant debris.
symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green areas on leaves
Leaf distortion, puckering, or curling
Stunted plant growth
Fruit may show internal browning or uneven ripening
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed
Plant resistant tomato varieties
Sanitize tools regularly with appropriate disinfectants
Wash hands thoroughly before handling plants
Avoid smoking near tomato plants (Tobacco Mosaic Virus can be transmitted this way)
Remove and destroy infected plants and debris
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.management: There is no cure for plants infected with ToMV. Management focuses on prevention through hygiene and resistant varieties. Infected plants should be removed. Consult a local agricultural expert for guidance.

Tomato___healthy.description: The leaf appears consistent with a healthy tomato plant based on the model's training data.
symptoms: No visible disease symptoms detected
prevention: Monitor regularly for early and late blight, bacterial spot, and whiteflies
Maintain good crop rotation, nutrition, and drainage practices
Tomato___healthy.management: Continue regular monitoring. Consult a local expert if any symptoms appear.
